papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, model, results (both tasks), discussion on decoherence; appendices skimmed only
papers.what_it_is: A proposal and numerical simulation of quantum reservoir computing using universal conductance fluctuations in mesoscopic conductors.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in numerical simulation on 500 cochleagrams from the NIST TI46 database (450 for training, 50 for testing) with all 4 gate voltages set to V = 5.9, the quantum transport reservoir reached 99.6% training and 94% testing accuracy on spoken-digit recognition.
assertions.anchor: Results, spoken-digit recognition, text and Fig. 3(c)
quotes: We obtain 500 cochleagrams from the NIST TI46 database, which are split into a training set of 450 and a testing set of 50.
Setting all 4 gate voltages to V = 5.9, the training result achieves a high recognition rate of 99.6% within about 50 epochs.
The highest training and testing results are 99.6% and 94%, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result of one simulated study, one test split of 50 samples.
assertions.reader_inference: The testing set is small (50 samples), so the 94% figure carries wide uncertainty.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for time-series forecasting, the NRMSEs are estimated at 0.043 for training and 0.047 for testing, and the training and testing NMSEs saturate at 0.0038 and 0.0042.
assertions.anchor: Results, time-series forecasting, and Discussion, Fig. 4
quotes: the NRMSEs are estimated to be 0.043 for training and 0.047 for testing.
In our work, the training and testing NMSEs saturate at 0.0038 and 0.0042, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulated result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they numerically demonstrate two benchmark tasks, spoken-digit recognition and time-series forecasting, to validate their proposal.
quotes: Leveraging universal conductance fluctuations, we numerically demonstrate two benchmark tasks, spoken-digit recognition and time-series forecasting, to validate our proposal.
assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract states the paper's own scope: a numerical demonstration.
assertions.reader_inference: The results are simulations, not a fabricated device.

assertions.value: The authors state that their scheme becomes ineffective when the encoding differences are smaller than the resolution limit of measurement.
quotes: Therefore, our scheme becomes ineffective when the encoding differences are smaller than the resolution limit of measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its limit, Discussion section.
